text: Bhupinder "Bindy" Singh Johal (January 14, 1971 – December 20, 1998) was an Indo-Canadian gangster from Vancouver, British Columbia, known as a self-confessed drug kingpin with a reputation for outspokenness, disregard for authority, and a long-standing rivalry with Robbie Kandola and the Dosanjh Brothers, who led a rival Punjabi Mafia faction. Johal operated alongside international drug lord Ranjit Cheema and controlled his own faction within the Punjabi Mafia, a loosely affiliated criminal organization originating in British Columbia that became increasingly ethnocentric over time and remained active and notorious in Vancouver since the early 1990s. He was born in 1971 (some sources note 1972 or 1973) in Shankar Nakodar, Punjab, India, to a Jatt Sikh family, and immigrated to Vancouver at age four, being raised by his mother after his parents separated. He was considered a "problem child" by teachers, displayed temperamental behavior, lacked respect for authority, and suffered severe depression after his parents cut his hair following an armed assault in Canada linked to the assassination of Indira Gandhi. He was expelled from Sir Charles Tupper Secondary School and sentenced to 60 days in jail in 1989 after assaulting his vice-principal, a defense he made that was dismissed by the judge as "cold-blooded cynicism" due to lack of evidence of racism. After moving to Richmond, he enrolled at McNair Secondary School, where he smashed a car window with a baseball bat and was convicted of possessing a dangerous weapon. He dropped out of college after his first semester to begin a criminal career, joining the Hispanic gang Los Diablos, which later became the Punjabi Mafia. He built a reputation as a hit-man for Jimmy and Ron Dosanjh, later betraying and killing both of them—Jimmy in February 1994 and Ron in April 1994—after the latter had taken out a contract to kill Johal for over C$230,000. The Dosanjh brothers were killed by men loyal to Johal, with Ron being shot in his red pickup truck while waiting for a traffic light and dying instantly from multiple bullets to the face. Johal was charged with two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the Dosanjh killings, along with Sarbjit Gill, Rajinder "Big Raj" Benji, Michael Kim Budai, Sun News Lai, Preet "Peter" Sarbjit Gill, and Kim "Phil" Ho-Sik, with the Crown alleging that Peter Gill was the actual gunman. The trial, one of the most expensive in Canadian history due to required security, resulted in acquittals for all defendants, including Gill, who was later convicted of obstruction of justice and sentenced to six years in prison; Gillian Guess, an active juror, was sentenced to 18 months for obstruction of justice. The Crown appealed the acquittals, but Johal was killed before a new trial began. Johal earned approximately $500,000 to $900,000 per week through illegal activities such as murder for hire, debt collection, and drug dealing, and was affiliated with the Buttar brothers, known for brutal gangland slayings. He formed a hit squad called "The Elite," consisting of five Indo-Canadian hit men, responsible for 25 murders over five years. Johal had a legendary bad temper, was convicted in 1997 of aggravated assault for attacking two men in a bar with a broken beer bottle, and had convictions for obstruction of justice, possession of dangerous weapons, and aggravated assault. In 1996, Chinese-Canadian drug dealer Randy Chan was kidnapped by Roman Mann, one of Johal’s associates, due to dissatisfaction with the quality of cocaine sold; Johal negotiated Chan’s release in exchange for 5 kilograms of cocaine and $500,000 from the Lotus triads. Johal openly admitted his gangster status and threatened rivals in interviews, becoming a folk hero among young Indo-Canadians who admired his success, wealth, and defiance of societal expectations, with many citing him as an inspiration to join organized crime. His gang was responsible for several murders, including the killing of Amarjit Singh Dheil in January 1997, Gorinder Singh Khun Khun on October 21, 1997 (after Johal believed Khun Khun was involved in the murder of neighbor Greg Olson), and Vinuse News MacKenzie on July 1, 1998, to eliminate a romantic rival. On September 19, 1998, Derek Chand Shankar insulted Johal, prompting Johal to order his murder after Buttar drove Shankar to the Queensborough Bridge, where he was shot. On November 29, 1998, Johal punched Roman "Danny" Mann after Mann expressed a desire to leave the gang, and Mann was later found dead in an industrial lot with a single bullet through his head; Johal blamed the Hells Angels. On December 20, 1998, at 4:30 a.m., Johal was fatally shot in the back of the head at the Palladium nightclub in Vancouver and died four hours later at Vancouver General Hospital. No witnesses described the assailant. Four months prior to his death, at least three of Johal’s associates had been killed, according to Bal Buttar’s confessions. In 2004, Buttar claimed he ordered Johal’s assassination out of fear that Johal would kill him. Buttar was never convicted of Johal’s murder due to his quadriplegic condition. Kash Heed, commanding officer of the 3rd Police District in Vancouver, stated it was disappointing that someone as intelligent and bright as Johal would turn to crime, noting that young people who emulate gangsters like Bindy see the benefits of criminal life without understanding the dangers.
